newsitem.title: GERMANY: Schmidt criticism of Bundesbank misguided - Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Schmidt criticism of Bundesbank misguided - Waigel.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel rejected criticism of the Bundesbank by former Chancellor Helmut Schmidt on Thursday and insisted on strict adherence to tough fiscal criteria for Europe's single currency.
Waigel, now straining to keep his 1997 budget within the strict Maastricht targets, said Schimdt was wrong to charge Germany with trying to play the monetary strong man in Europe.

He said a more flexible interpretation of Maastricht's guidelines, which Schmidt called for on Thursday in the Die Zeit weekly he co-publishes, would weaken the new euro currency and lead Germans to reject it as inferior to the mark.

"Schmidt's criticism of us and Tietmeyer is misguided and wrong," Waigel told German radio. "I don't know who in the last few decades has been acting like a megalomaniac in Europe and the world -- I certainly haven't been."

The blast from Schmidt, the Social Democratic chancellor from 1974 until Christian Democrat Helmut Kohl replaced him in 1982, had as much to do with settling old political scores as it did with debating the best path to the single currency.

The sharp-tongued ex-chancellor, a regular critic of Kohl and Tietmeyer, recalled in his bitter article the Bundesbank president had been part of the political intrigues in 1982 that led the small Free Democratic Party to abandon him for Kohl.
The full-page article showed a picture of Schmidt, 77, in a familiar pose -- raising a warning index finger -- and another photograph of Tietmeyer with a hand cupped over one ear.

Reflecting what some Europeans might be thinking, Schmidt said Tietmeyer's insistence that participants in European economic and monetary union (EMU) toe a strict fiscal line upset Germans and made them unpopular abroad.
Schmidt said Tietmeyer's insistence that members meet the targets strictly ignored manoeuvring room in the Maastricht treaty and put an ugly face on Germany's European policies.
"The Germany you represent appears power-hungry and too mighty to many of our neighbors," wrote Schmidt, who has in the past also accused Kohl of flexing Germany's muscles.

"The insistent and overpowering nature of your speeches not only makes you unpopular -- which you can certainly bear -- but rather makes Germany as a whole unloved, something we have not deserved and cannot endure."
In a letter to Tietmeyer earlier this year, he wrote: "I regard you as the most significant opponent of currency union."
Asked to comment, a spokesman would only say: "The Bundesbank is opposed to dealing with these accusations again."

Bonn argues it must insist on fiscal discipline to convince financial markets and a wary German public that the benefits of monetary union outweigh the risks. Tietmeyer says he is pro-European but concerned about stability.
Many Germans are luke-warm on EMU. They do not want to give up their strong mark for the unknown Euro, fearing it could lead to a repeat of the hyperinflation of the 1920s.
The German government has also met resistance from trade unions and opposition parties to its efforts to trim budget deficits in order to meet EMU targets next year.

The criteria limiting budget deficits and public debt are so strict that even Germany has so far failed to meet them, fuelling speculation that the criteria might have to be weakened to ensure monetary union takes place at all.

In the article, written in the tone of wounded pride Schmidt has taken since being outmaneouvered by Kohl, the ex-chancellor insinuated Tietmeyer was so tough on EMU because he did not want to lose his powerful job.
"It's not nice to be demoted from the de facto currency king to a branch director of the European Central Bank," he wrote. "The thrust of your arguments is to hinder that."
